newsitem.title: Australia: TELECOMS - Optus sees big business from data.
newsitem.headline: TELECOMS - Optus sees big business from data.

text.p: Australian telecommunications carrier Optus Communications said it expects strong growth for on-line services and electronic banking to make data-based communications the largest single telecom market in Australia.
"I think the market will eventually be bigger than all forms of voice communications," Optus chief executive officer Zygmunt Switkowski told Reuters in an interview.
"We have got some internal numbers, but it would be fair to say that is an area for which we would aim for the highest growth over the near term," Switkowski said.

He said the sector's growth was due to increasing use by companies of data-based services, financial transactions through EFTPOS (Electronic Funds Transfer at Point Of Sale), telephone bill-payments and electronic mail (E-mail).
The telecom market among Australia's corporate and government services is worth about A$2 billion (US$1.58 billion) or about 17 percent of the nation's A$12 billion total telecommunications market.

"Whether companies, institutions or government departments are video-conferencing, sending email, sending data and connecting to the Internet,...it is going to be a big opportunity surely," said Switkowski.

Optus' business network services (BNS), which caters for the corporate market, reported sales growth of 59 percent to A$233 million in the year to June 30, 1996. Although this only makes up 12 percent of Optus' total A$1.94 billion 1995/96 revenue, the BNS unit is the group's fastest growing sector.
Optus is expected to raise more than A$1.0 billion from a share market float later in 1996 through the issue of new shares and the selldown of shares from existing shareholders.
"After the float, we will have A$2.2 billion of equity and A$2.2 billion of debt and we will keep that one-to-one ratio more or less in that range," said Switkowski.
"With that amount of money and increasing retention of our profits that will keep the company growing nicely for some period of time," he said.
The deregulation of the telecommunications market in Australia on July 1, 1997 could present more opportunities for Optus, he said.
"I think the growth rates we have achieved in recent years, could easily be stimulated in a deregulatory environment."
He said carriers that want to offer telephony services in Australia might have to use Optus' telephone network infrastructure, which would mean more customers and revenue.

Optus' 46.5 percent-owned Optus Vision is spending A$3.0 billion on rolling out its fibre-optic cable network in order to carry local telephony services and have a competing network with Telstra's telephone network infrastructure.
"Those sort of companies need to make a decision on whether they want to build their own infrastructure or simply buy access to the current infrastructure which will carry," Switkowski said
"Our strategy would be to make it attractive to those companies to become our customers," he said.
"In many ways deregulation with the arrival of range new service providers customers will extend Optus' customer base."
No telecommunications carriers have yet formally announced that they would enter Australia's telephone call market, but increased competition is expected in the long distance and local call markets.
"There will be casualities in competition over the next few years. There will be a bit of a sorting out," Switkowski said.

Optus is 25 percent owned by Mayne Nickless Ltd, 24.5 percent each owned by BellSouth Corp of the United States and Cable and Wireless Plc of Britain, while Australian institutional investors own the rest.
